sections.brief: The three wartime promises (Hussein–McMahon, Sykes–Picot, Balfour) and why Britain wanted Palestine: the route to India, Suez, oil. The drafting of the Balfour Declaration, Montagu's opposition, Walter Rothschild as addressee (two-Rothschilds distinction). Figures: a timeline of the three promises; a comparison of what each promise said and to whom.

Allenby's entry into Jerusalem (11 Dec 1917), his proclamation, military administration (OETA), Ronald Storrs as governor of Jerusalem and the Pro-Jerusalem Society. What the occupation meant in practice before any Mandate existed.

The Faisal–Weizmann Agreement of 3 January 1919: text, Faisal's handwritten condition, whether it lapsed, and how each side has used it since. Figure: comparison of what the agreement offered and the condition attached.
The Paris Peace Conference in 1919 as it touched Palestine; the King–Crane Commission, what it found and why its report was shelved.

By what right: how a British letter became international law. Article 22 of the League Covenant, the mandate system, the class A mandates, and the debate over whether Palestine's mandate departed from Article 22. Figure: process flow from letter to League instrument.

The Palestinian national movement: Muslim-Christian Associations, the Palestine Arab Congresses, the Arab Executive, the delegations to London, their demands, and Britain's answers. Include Palestinian political agency and internal divisions as the sources document them. Figure: timeline of the congresses.
The Third Aliyah, 1919–1923: who came, from where, how many (with the disputed range), the labor movement, kibbutzim and Gdud HaAvoda; immigration quotas. Figure: key figures.

Nebi Musa (April 1920) and Jaffa (May 1921), the founding of the Haganah, Jabotinsky's arrest and sentence, the end of the Jewish Legion, and Britain's first two inquiries (Palin, Haycraft) and what they concluded.
Keren Hayesod (1920): fundraising made permanent; how the money moved and what it built. Figure: money chain.

Herbert Samuel's appointment of Amin al-Husseini as Mufti of Jerusalem (1921) and the creation of the Supreme Muslim Council: how it happened, the disputed account of the vote, and why Britain did it. Figure: power structure of Muslim institutions under the Mandate.

Kings by appointment: the Cairo Conference of 1921, Faisal in Iraq, Abdullah in Transjordan, and Sharif Hussein's refusal to sign Versailles or the Anglo-Hejazi treaty; what this shows about the wartime promises. Keep Iran's 1921 coup brief (it belongs to another volume) and link forward.

The separation of Transjordan (1921–1922), the Transjordan memorandum, Revisionist rejection (Jabotinsky, 'two banks of the Jordan'), and the later claim that 'Jordan is already Palestine' made by both sides, with its history to 1988 and today.
The Churchill White Paper of June 1922: what it said, the absorptive-capacity rule, how each side received it, and what happened to population growth anyway.

The Mandate for Palestine (approved 24 July 1922): the text's key articles from the primary document, Palestine as a named polity (citizenship, passports, currency), the Jewish Agency clause, and what the text gave and withheld. Figures: power structure of Mandate government; comparison of Balfour 1917 and the Mandate 1922.
The first American fundraising and political campaigns, 1921–22: Weizmann and Einstein's tour, the Brandeis split, Sokolow and Harding.
The Lodge–Fish Resolution (1922): who lobbied for it, who opposed it (including the State Department), and what it did and did not commit the United States to.

The 1922 Legislative Council proposal: composition, why the Zionist side accepted and the Arab side refused, the 1923 boycott, and Britain's later attempts. Figure: comparison of the council as offered and the objections.
Who actually ran Palestine: the seven High Commissioners (1920–1948) and the office itself. Close the stage structurally. Figure: timeline of the seven, and a power structure of the office.
